I think the thing non-mathematicians and non-CS people who only know complexity theory vaguely need to remember is that complexity theory has nothing to do with reality.

A 2^64bits lookup table only has O(1) lookup if you ignore the impossibility of creating a machine that has 2 exabytes of storage where all those bytes have the same access time. Or you'd have to redefine O(1) to be “at most the worst case”. But strictly speaking from the mathematical definition it’s O(1). Which is why no one in practical engineering takes most complexity results seriously as the entire field maps to practice poorly precisely for these reasons (all our machines use fixed integer math and have limited tape storage)

children.author: tgv
children.text:
> You can always always tradeoff time vs space

Not always, isn't it? The theorem says that there exists a function that can be sped up, but not that every function can be. A trivial counter example would be the identity function on a TM. It's simply a HALT/ACCEPT. There's no way to reduce that.

The space/time trade-off is also not infinitely flexible, since it takes time to fill space. And lookup tables have to be constructed at run-time, or they'll be of finite size, and hence only a constant speed-up. Perhaps you were thinking of that theorem, the linear as wikipedia calls it? https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_speedup_theorem

children.author: openasocket
children.text:
It’s been a while since I studied complexity theory, but is that what Blums speed up theorem says? A quick google search suggests it states that there exist computable functions where there is no optimal program that computes it.

Like, there exist problems that have a lower bound of n time where algorithms can get arbitrarily close to O(n) complexity but there is no program that actually reaches it (there is one that runs in time O(n^{1.1}), one that runs in O(n^{1.01}), etc).

But that doesn’t mean that there aren’t hard walls, it just means there are hard walls where every program’s runtime is > that wall, rather than >= that wall. But maybe I’m misunderstanding, or there are some corollaries I’m missing?

As an aside, as someone who studied more on the pure math side, Blums speed up theorem is rather intuitive. It looks like there might be a relatively elegant proof using topology. Blums speed up theorem is basically just a statement that the set of programs that implement a particular computable function doesn’t satisfy the greatest lower bound property. This is also the case for, for example, the set of rational numbers: there exist subsets of the rational numbers with a lower bound but not a greatest lower bound (like the set of all positive rational numbers q where q^2 >= 2). I’m hand waving, but I think in that same vein you can show that the set of programs under the topology of ordering by runtime is completely disconnected.

children.author: fooker
children.text:
You can’t put everything in a lookup table with the lookup cost being O(1).

If the things you have to memoize are super-linear, suppose you need to store some value related to all subsets of an input set of size n.

There’s no way you can do this in O(1), even assuming infinitely large memory.

The site is taking forever to load but complexity theory doesn't really have the hard walls at things like O(nlogn) that people seem to think.

You can always always tradeoff time vs space. It's actually a fundamental part of complexity theory called Blums speedup theorem by the guy who invented complexity theory no less.

As an example you give me an nlogn solution and i take a portion of the inner loop, put it in a lookup table (who cares if the lookup table is 2^n in size, that's not what we're measuring here since we're specifically measuring time not space) and suddenly i have something better than nlogn since that lookup table is O(1).

That's not to say there's some merit to all of this. It's just that people shouldn't be as astonished by these results as they are. It's complexity theory. There's literally no such thing as a hard wall where something is nlogn in time and can't get lower. It can always get lower. But you need both the time and space complexities together to reason about this.

children.author: ssivark
children.text:
The string comparison model is useful in the regime where string lengths are much shorter than list lengths and can be bounded by a constant. It would be a horribly broken (i.e. unrepresentative) model if you were constructing intermediate strings whose lengths could grow arbitrarily and become much longer than list lengths.

One can of course make a puzzle out of anything, but it behooves asking what situation is being modelled by that problem.

And yes, this criticism might apply more broadly to TCS rather than just this specific artifact from OpenAI. It's reward hacking regardless of whether humans do it or LLMs.

This is a very loaded blog post. A unit-cost RAM is a fairly standard model of computation when working with algorithms. When we say that comparison sorting of strings takes O(n log n) time, for instance, we are also implicitly assuming a unit cost for comparing two strings. In real life, comparing two strings scales linearly with string length. Maybe that's silly, but it's par for the course. The original FFT is also assuming unit cost multiplication when we say it is O(n log n) time - we mean O(n log n) multiplies.

Similarly, yes, it's a galactic algorithm, but these things are still viewed as meaningful. The fact that it is even possible at all with a unit cost RAM asymptotically is an incredible result that nobody expected.

Ben Recht has a nice blog post about how these results are basically reward hacking the TCS formalization by assuming atomic operations for exact complex arithmetic, instead of costs scaling with the size/precision of the number: https://www.argmin.net/p/faster-fourier-transforms

number multiplication is basically convolution and closely tied with FFTs, so I wouldn't personally be surprised even if a lot of the "FFT's work" could somehow be stuffed into exact arithmetic operations, and the remaining costs just track the packing and unpacking from that representation. It's just an exploit of the book-keeping.

That's ignoring the other complaints about this being a galactic algorithm.

Is there any good writeup yet of intuitively where the speedup comes from? E.g. with fast fourier transform you can see that there's a lot of symmetry & recomputation in the Vandermonde matrix, so that's where the speed up comes from.

children.text: Look at the citations on the graph, the agents are trying off the wall ideas like 30 dimensional geometry and E8. If any of these ideas are particularly fruitful, humans can retroactively use their very limited attention and build it into a mathematical cannon. The take away from this is that we getting to see an early instance of a distributed agent swarm relentlessly work a hard problem with progress that can be tracked by a simple metric (maximize kappa).

No offense to the participants, but TBH I believe this is exactly the moment what Terrence Tao was concerning on "vibemathing". OpenAI breaking the O(N log N) barrier could be a meaningful event and surprise mathematicians and we have valuable information that it was not a lower bound indeed. I'm afraid that in this autoresearch campaign people are focusing only on lowering numbers, while having insights that humans can learn.
